skill.name: truth-layer
skill.description: Verification workflow for validating claims, finding blockers, and reporting project status with evidence.
skill.summary: Validate completion claims and surface unresolved blockers before progress is reported.
skill.author: CleanExpo

security_audit.summary: All 12 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown code fences or inline command formatting, not Ruby or shell backtick execution. The skill is mainly a verification workflow, but it tells agents to automatically use MCP tools and Bash when blocked, which creates a medium tool-use risk. No evidence of prompt injection or data exfiltration intent was found.

remediation.issue: Automatic MCP and Bash usage guidance
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user confirmation before running Bash commands or MCP inspections, and define the allowed command scope.
Clarify that the skill cannot override system, developer, or user instructions when deciding whether work can proceed.

finding_verdicts.reason: Lines 44-54 are a Markdown code fence containing a blocker report template. There is no executable Ruby or shell backtick execution.
The finding covers Markdown structure around a closed code fence and workflow heading. It is documentation text, not executable command invocation.
Lines 59-72 show a TypeScript-style result shape inside a Markdown code block. The content is illustrative and contains no shell execution path.
This range is Markdown text around the end of the example and the claim verification checklist. It does not execute commands through Ruby or shell backticks.
The inline backticks format a hardcoded npm typecheck command in documentation. It is command guidance, but not dynamic backtick execution or user-controlled command construction.
Lines 83-96 are a Markdown report format template. The fenced block is plain documentation and is not executable code.
The range contains the close of a Markdown example and surrounding prose. No command interpreter or backtick execution mechanism is present.
Lines 102-108 are an ASCII flow diagram inside a Markdown fence. The arrows and labels are descriptive text, not shell syntax.
This range includes prose about MCP and Bash usage, but the detected backticks are Markdown formatting. The tool-use concern is handled separately as a semantic finding.
Lines 140-149 are an example blocker report in a Markdown code fence. It contains no executable command or shell expansion.
The finding points to Markdown fence boundaries and a section heading. This is presentation syntax, not a command execution primitive.
Lines 152-156 are a quoted bad-report example inside a Markdown fence. The text is illustrative and cannot execute commands.

semantic_findings.title: Automatic Command and Tool Use Guidance
semantic_findings.description: The skill tells the agent that when blocked it should automatically use Playwright, filesystem, git MCP, and Bash to run build commands. This can expand tool usage without an explicit confirmation step in sensitive repositories.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The text directly instructs automatic MCP and Bash usage, but it does not specify destructive commands or data exfiltration. The risk is bounded to tool invocation and project inspection.

content.value_statement: Teams can overstate progress when builds, tests, and type checks are not verified. This skill gives Claude, Codex, and Claude Code a structured review process for honest blocker reporting.
actual_capabilities: Validates status claims against build, test, and typecheck evidence.
Identifies blockers with impact, root cause, current state, and next action.
Separates claimed outcomes from observed project reality.
Encourages UI, filesystem, and git history inspection when tools are available.
Provides structured formats for blocker and verification reports.
Flags stub tests, unresolved dependencies, and incomplete validation.
limitations: It does not replace full quality assurance or security review.
It needs access to code, logs, tests, or tool output to verify claims.
It may slow delivery by blocking unresolved issues.
Tool and command use still require appropriate user approval and environment permissions.

use_cases.title: Validate Delivery Claims
use_cases.description: Check whether a feature is truly complete before status is reported to stakeholders.

use_cases.title: Stop Release Blockers Early
use_cases.description: Identify build, dependency, migration, or type errors before release work continues.

use_cases.title: Audit Agent Work
use_cases.description: Review AI-generated progress reports against real files, tests, and command results.

prompt_templates.title: Check a Completion Claim
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the truth-layer process to verify this claim: [paste claim]. Compare the claim with the available evidence and report any blockers.

prompt_templates.title: Find Hidden Blockers
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the current project state for blockers before progress continues. Check build status, tests, type errors, dependencies, and missing evidence.

prompt_templates.title: Review Test Quality
prompt_templates.prompt: Assess whether the tests prove the feature works. Identify stub tests, skipped tests, missing assertions, and claims that are not supported.

prompt_templates.title: Run a Full Truth Pass
prompt_templates.prompt: Perform a full truth-layer audit for this workstream. Validate all completion claims, list unresolved blockers, rank impact, and state what must happen next.

output_examples.input: A developer says the feature is ready, but only a typecheck log is available.
output_examples.output: The report states that readiness is not verified. It lists missing test evidence, unknown runtime behavior, and the next check required.

output_examples.input: A release manager asks whether deployment can continue after a build warning.
output_examples.output: The response treats the warning as unresolved until reviewed. It explains deployment impact and names the owner action needed to unblock.

output_examples.input: An AI agent reports that tests passed, but the test file appears empty.
output_examples.output: The response flags the test result as unsupported. It separates the claimed success from the actual empty test coverage.

best_practices: Provide the claim, expected evidence, and recent command output.
Run checks in a safe project environment before accepting conclusions.
Resolve blocker root causes before reporting work as complete.
anti_patterns: Using the skill to approve work without running requested checks.
Treating warnings, skipped tests, or empty tests as success.
Allowing automatic commands in sensitive repositories without review.

faq.question: What does this skill verify?
faq.answer: It verifies project status claims against evidence such as builds, tests, type checks, dependencies, and file state.

faq.question: Does it run tests by itself?
faq.answer: It can guide an agent to request or run checks when tools are available, but user permissions still control execution.

faq.question: Can it prove a release is production ready?
faq.answer: No. It can identify missing evidence and blockers, but final release approval still needs human review.

faq.question: Why does it block progress?
faq.answer: It blocks progress when evidence shows unresolved build, test, type, dependency, or migration issues.

faq.question: Is this useful for Claude Code and Codex?
faq.answer: Yes. It gives Claude Code and Codex a shared verification checklist for coding workflow status.

faq.question: What evidence should I provide?
faq.answer: Provide the claim, changed files, command outputs, test results, build logs, and any known risks or skipped checks.
